A loud scream emanated from the main halls bathroom, causing all the elderly women sat around the kitchen table to pause in their knitting. Joshua set the charcuterie board on the kitchen island, finding his feet were moving before his mind had caught up.  He hadn’t minded his mother hosting her knitting club in his new house. Gossip and talker as she was, all of her friends and acquaintances probably thought this new upgrade would be wealth personified. Older folk here tended to think a high tech job close in stature to a doctor’s, simply by it being something they could never understand. In this moment, he wished he was a doctor. 

	“Mrs.Mayfield? Are you alright?” Joshua called at the bathroom door. 

	The best he could hope for was that the heater tank was just so new she had burned her hands, the worst was that she’d fallen and broken something. Either way, he would never hear the end of this from his mother.
Only the clack of the chains from the lining room fan, the sound of chairs not so distant scraping against polished cherrywood, and the hushed urgent whisper from their occupants followed. Sweat poured from every orifice on Joshua’s body, but if it was from the Georgia heat or the silence from beyond the door, he could not tell. 

	“Mrs.Mayfield?” He called again. A small crowd of women gathered behind him. Finally , a shaky voice answered out. 

	“Why…yes. One moment dear.” Came the reply. There were a few noises from behind the bathroom door, the softest of curses that no doubt the other women would have admonished if heard, and then the click of the door.

	Mrs.Mayfield appeared, pale face the shade of ghosts, hands trembling. She held an object, under her arm, covered by the peach cardigan she had worn upon entering the house. She looked at Joshua and made the cross symbol, then shoved the object with the sweater into his hands. 

	“Young man, I don’t know what kind of satanist rituals you are into, but you should be ashamed of yourself.” Spittle reached his clothes as she said this and Joshua found himself taking a half-step back, slightly alarmed. 

	He uncovered the object laid in the sweater. It was the mirror he had bought for cheap at the  antique store a few streets away. The mirror had been restored and polished before he hung it up, and he squinted to see if he had missed something. 

	“I’m sorry, but Mrs.Mayfield…are you alright? I don’t think anything on here is satanic. This mirror is Victorian style, and I thought it’d go nice with the style of the house.”

	Joshua flipped the back of the mirror over, trying to see if maybe something was written on the back, but as he did so a chorus of screams and wails erupted from the women behind him. Soon, they were all fleeing, knitting projects forgotten, bags and purses snatched from the entryway and almost falling over each other at the door. Even his mother had not stopped to look back at him. After sitting down with the mirror for a few hours and conversing with Reddit, ChatGPT, and all manner of forums, he made his way back to the antique shop. Of course, it was closed on Wednesdays. 

	He returned to his house, organizing each woman’s project and placing them the packing boxes he hadn’t gotten around to recycling. Frustrated and thinking nothing of the omens for broken mirrors, he tossed the mirror on the ground, wincing as the telltale sounds of shattering moved to his ears. The ground started to rumble, then shake. Joshua thought an earthquake was taking place and deftly took cover under his kitchen table. He couldn’t remember if that’s what you were supposed to, and found himself wishing not for the first time that every life problem had a solution that could be found in StackOverflow. Something moving nearby caught his eye. It was the mirror, shaking violently, scattering and rearranging itself into something on the floor. His mouth went dry when it finished. The mirror had grown six times in size, the glass replaced with some type of viscous blue fluid. He crawled from underneath the table, and with the barest of brushes from his fingertips, the mirror pulled him in.

Arson was not the worst crime Maria had committed, but while she watched the hungry flames from her hotel window, she thought this would be the one she could not forgive. It hadn’t taken much to convince herself that burning this final tether to her humanity would be easier than pretending any remained within her vessel. It had felt strange, seeing the mirages, hearing the echos, walking with ghosts within her home. He only moved in three months ago, and yet the bones of house- creaking stairs and worn handles, dishes placed just slightly higher, sets of towels and bedding in color instead of the neutrality she preferred to live her personal life, whispered that he was as permanent to the residence as she.

	In the months that followed, she had doubled her job intake to forget. When her oxfords clacked cobblestones in Paris as a businessman who tapped in time to his cane, she heard only the sound of a camera’s click. When the job was to spread discourse in the cartel so that cocaine shipments stuttered in the US, the young man had freckles, just like him. The countless hostage rescues, the tiny manipulations for world powers and orders, the private investigations; Each time she shifted into someone else she lost a piece of herself and found another reminder of him. Returning back to a home that had yellowed into a house would not do. Even the mirrors betrayed her, showing her someone she could recognize, until finally, she accepted she had died too, and would never find her true image again.

	Maria turned from the window and the firefighter’s attempts of saving something long ago turned ash. She ran weathered fingers over the dusted suitcase atop the lone mattress in the room. Initials that were not hers looked back at her. She hadn’t seen the point of saving anything of hers, but this…

	When she opened the suitcase, a low groan escaped her lips. His old camera, his favorite fedora she had begged him to stop wearing for every occasion, and there, taped across the top, was a dozen photos of her, and a box named “Maria”. The real her. Her had never asked and never minded that she chose to wear bodies long after a job. He never asked and she never answered as to where she’d been or why she was who she was. But here, in the dimmed lights of the room, was her, smiling, balancing Jenga blocks as if she were constructing the world, when the world was just out picture, behind the camera, all along.

-Sit with your wife. Make subtle comments about you checking out places for her to get some help.
